title: GTA 6 Recording Audio: 3 Checks Before You Upload
description: Recording GTA 6 for YouTube, TikTok, or Instagram? Find the Mute Licensed Music setting, run a 10-second mic and game-audio test, and listen to your final export before you post. Includes a tip for recording your mic and game audio on separate tracks. Independent GTA 6 commentary with original analysis and synthetic narration.

chapters.title: Three things to check
lines: You're about to capture a clip in Grand Theft Auto Six. You can hear your mic, the game sounds fine, and the take looks clean.
Then you listen back and realize the music is baked into the same file as the moment you wanted to share.
There are three checks that make this easier. First, check what the game sends to your recorder.
Second, listen to what your recorder actually saved. Third, look at every sound you added after you hit stop.
I'll walk through the menu, the ten-second capture test, and how I would set up a voice-over without losing the game sounds.

chapters.title: Where the setting lives
chapters.short_title: GTA 6: Where to Find Mute Licensed Music
lines: Before capturing GTA six, open the pause menu, go to Settings, and select Audio.
Rockstar calls the switch Mute Licensed Music. Turn it on before you start.
Picture an audio wire running from the game into your capture. Changing the setting now changes what reaches the next file.
If you already captured a track with music mixed into it, flipping the switch later leaves that old clip as it was.
That's why I put this step at the top of the checklist, before I find the moment I want to keep.
chapters.short_description: Here’s where to find Mute Licensed Music in GTA 6. Check the setting before recording, then play back a short clip to hear what your capture actually picked up.

chapters.title: The ten-second test
chapters.short_title: GTA 6 Recording: Do This 10-Second Audio Test
lines: Here's a ten-second test you can run before capturing GTA six. Start a local capture and say one sentence at your normal volume.
Let some ordinary game sound play underneath it. Stop the capture and open the actual file.
Ask three questions. Can I understand every word? Can I still hear what happened in the game? Did I capture any music I didn't expect?
Listening to the file catches problems a live monitor can miss. Once the mix sounds right, you're ready to capture the real clip.
chapters.short_description: Before recording GTA 6, capture 10 seconds and play it back. Listen for your mic, dialogue, effects, and any music your recorder picked up.

chapters.title: Two tracks make editing easier
lines: If your capture setup can save separate audio tracks, try one for the game and one for the microphone.
Think of those as two faders. If an engine drowns out the first few words of a sentence, you can turn the game down just for those words.
With everything already on one track, lowering the game also lowers your voice. A separate voice-over added afterwards can solve the same problem.
For a short clip, I would keep the game sound around the action, then bring it down for the one thing I want the viewer to notice.
Make the point while the moment is on screen. That gives the viewer something to look for as they hear it.

chapters.title: Check the final export
chapters.short_title: What GTA 6’s Mute Licensed Music Setting Actually Does
lines: Turning on Mute Licensed Music in Grand Theft Auto Six helps with the audio the game sends into your next capture.
Now check the rest of the export. A song added in your editor comes from a different source.
If you're making one file for Shorts, Reels, and TikTok, use narration and sound you can publish on all three.
Then listen to that final file from start to finish. The menu setting is step one. The file you're about to upload is the real test.
chapters.short_description: Changing Mute Licensed Music affects future GTA 6 recordings. Listen to your finished export to check the audio your viewers will hear.

chapters.title: A checklist for the next take
lines: Here's the checklist for the next take. Set the game audio before you start. Play back a short capture. Listen again after you export.
A separate check is permission to use the footage commercially. Rockstar's general fan-footage policy describes non-commercial use. Read it before building a monetized video around game footage.
I made this walkthrough with original diagrams because the audio question is easier to see as a simple path.
Game to recorder, recorder to edit, edit to upload. Find the stage where a sound enters the file, and you'll know where to fix it.
